notes.b: A physical activity biography is the story of how a person has been active so far and what they do now. Writing one shows what has shaped a person's habits, which is the first step in understanding participation.
points: History content: the activities taken up and given up, the age at each, and the settings used (school, club, home, outdoors), so you can see how a person's activity changed over time.
History content: the influences on participation, such as family, school, friends, coaches and facilities, because these often explain why someone started, kept going or stopped.
History content: the reasons for starting and stopping each activity, and the high and low points, such as a first team win or an injury that ended a sport.
Presentation: a timeline by life stage (for example childhood, early teens, senior cycle) that marks the turning points, where a person's activity changed direction.
Current profile: the activities done now, how often, for how long and at what intensity (how hard the effort is). This is the person's activity profile today.

Comparison: set the biography beside someone whose profile differs, such as a non-participant, an older adult or someone with a disability, and explain the differences in influences, opportunities and motivation.
notes.tip: You present your own biography and one for a person whose activity profile differs from yours. For the second person, explain why the two profiles differ, not just how.

notes.b: A support is something that makes it easier to be active and a barrier is something that makes it harder. School shapes activity for most young people, so it has both.
points: Support: PE classes taught by qualified teachers and coaches, who make activity enjoyable and accessible so pupils build skill and confidence.
Support: school teams and extra-curricular activities (those outside timetabled classes), such as after-school clubs, which give pupils regular chances to take part.
Support: lunchtime leagues and activity breaks during the school day, which fit activity into time pupils are already in school.
Support: facilities and equipment that are available to pupils outside class time, so activity is not limited to the PE timetable.
Support: the Active School Flag, a Department of Education initiative that recognises schools that promote physical activity and PE, and a positive peer culture that values activity.
Barrier: limited time for PE on the timetable, and exam pressure, especially in senior cycle, which leads pupils to give up activity to study.
Barrier: a narrow range of activities, with a focus on competitive sports that some pupils do not enjoy, so they feel there is nothing for them.
Barrier: lack of facilities or limited access to them, changing-room and kit concerns that discourage some pupils, and low confidence in one's own skill or body.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to describe supports in school other than PE classes, so know several, such as teams, clubs, lunchtime leagues and facilities, and say how each helps.

notes.h: Supports and barriers in the community
notes.b: Outside school, whether a person is active depends on what is available locally and whether they can afford and reach it. The community also offers supports and barriers.
points: Support: local clubs and sports partnerships offering organised activity, which give people a place to train and play with others.
Support: parks, greenways (traffic-free routes for walking and cycling) and walking routes that are free to use, so cost is not an obstacle.
Support: free events, such as parkrun (a free weekly 5 km timed event on Saturday mornings) and fun runs, which welcome beginners.
Support: family involvement, such as parents driving children to sessions and attending them, which gives encouragement and solves transport.
Support: accessible and affordable facilities close to home, which make regular activity realistic.
Barrier: cost of membership, fees and equipment, which can exclude people on low incomes.
Barrier: transport, especially where public transport is limited or travel to facilities is long, and lack of local facilities.
Barrier: safety concerns, such as poorly lit paths, opening hours that do not suit people who work or study, and weather, which stops outdoor activity.
Barrier: lack of programmes for some groups, so those people have nothing suitable to join.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to outline two supports and two barriers in the community, or to discuss two barriers. For each one, say how it helps or stops participation, not just name it. Keep to school and community in general here.

notes.b: Every school or community factor falls into one of four types. Sorting factors this way helps you see what kind of action would fix a problem.
points: Personal: time, motivation, confidence, skill level, injury and body image, which all depend on the individual.
Social: family, friends and culture, which can either encourage or discourage participation depending on whether they value activity.
Environmental: facilities, transport, safety and weather, which are about the places and conditions around a person.
Economic: membership fees, equipment and travel costs, which decide whether a person can afford to take part.
notes.tip: When asked to group factors, use the four headings personal, social, environmental and economic, and place each factor under the right one.

notes.b: To understand participation you need evidence, and no single method records everything. Each method collects a different type of information and has its own strength and limitation.
points: Pedometers record steps per day. Strength: cheap and objective (not based on opinion). Limitation: they do not record cycling, swimming or intensity.
Activity diaries or logs record the type, duration and intensity of each activity. Strength: detailed. Limitation: they depend on honesty and memory, so entries may be wrong.

Questionnaires and surveys record self-reported activity and attitudes from many people quickly. Strength: wide reach. Limitation: self-report bias, because people may overstate or forget their activity.
Interviews and focus groups record reasons and attitudes in depth. Strength: they explain why people do or do not take part. Limitation: time-consuming and limited to small numbers.
Wearable trackers and smartphone apps record steps, heart rate and distance. Strength: automatic and continuous, so nothing relies on memory. Limitation: cost and accuracy limits.
Heart-rate monitors record the intensity of activity. Strength: they show whether activity is moderate or vigorous. Limitation: cost, and the need to wear them correctly.

Observation and attendance records count numbers using a facility or club. Strength: objective counts that do not rely on memory. Limitation: they show whether people attend, but not why or how active they are.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to name methods and say what information each collects, to identify three methods, or to suggest methods for a survey. Always pair the method with the information it records, plus a strength and a limitation.

notes.h: Analysing participation patterns in a group
notes.b: A specific group in the school community, such as a year group or girls in senior cycle, can be analysed in five steps. Once you have the steps, you can also check the results against patterns that are commonly found.
points: Step 1: collect data on the group, using a questionnaire, activity diary or attendance record.
Step 2: present the data in tables and bar charts so that comparisons between activities and groups are clear.
Step 3: describe the patterns, such as which activities are most popular, how often students take part and any drop-off (fall in participation) with age.
Step 4: explain the likely reasons, such as exam pressure, interests, cost, facilities or gender.
Step 5: suggest actions the school could take, linked to the reasons found, so the suggestions fit the problem.
Common pattern: participation falls through adolescence, especially in senior cycle, often because of exam pressure and changing interests.
Common pattern: team-sport participation is often higher among boys, while drop-out is often higher among girls. This is one observed pattern only.
Common pattern: popular activities reflect local facilities and traditions, such as strong Gaelic games participation where clubs are local, and low swimming where there is no pool.
notes.tip: When you interpret school survey data, explain the differences between activities and year groups, not just describe them, and link each difference to a likely reason such as facilities or exams.

notes.b: Promotion means encouraging more people to be active. Different approaches work at different levels, from national campaigns to a single school.
points: National media campaigns reach large audiences through television, radio and social media.
School-based programmes, such as the Active School Flag (a Department of Education initiative recognising schools that promote physical activity and PE), daily activity breaks and PE.
Community events, such as parkrun (a free weekly 5 km timed event on Saturday mornings) and fun runs.
Targeted programmes for groups with low participation, which aim to help where it is most needed.
Making environments active, such as building greenways and cycle lanes, so being active becomes the easy choice.
Incentives and free access, such as free taster sessions or free entry to events, which remove cost as a barrier.
Role models, such as athletes and coaches, who inspire others to take part.
Wearable technology and challenges, such as step challenges that track progress and keep people motivated.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to discuss two approaches to promotion. Pick two, say how each works and give an example from this list.

notes.b: Evaluating an approach means judging how well it works. Five questions help you decide.
points: Reach: how many people take part, and whether they are the people the approach targeted.
Cost: the money, staff and facilities needed, compared with the number of people reached, which shows whether it is good value.
Sustainability: whether activity continues once the programme ends, because a short burst of activity does little for long-term health.
Inactive groups: whether the approach reaches people who are not active, not only those already keen, since those are the people who gain most.
Measuring success: participation records, questionnaires or trackers used before and after the programme to show change.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to evaluate measures of a programme's success. Name how success is measured, such as participation records, questionnaires or trackers, and say why a before-and-after comparison shows change.

notes.h: How a school can increase participation
notes.b: A school can act directly on the barriers pupils face. Each action below targets a barrier covered earlier, such as a narrow range of activities or low confidence.
points: Offer a wider range of activities, so pupils with different interests can find one they enjoy.
Provide non-competitive options, such as fitness classes or walking groups, for pupils who dislike competitive sport.
Run lunchtime and after-school clubs, which give extra chances to be active outside class.
Let students have a say in which activities are offered, so they are more likely to take part in them.
Link with local clubs, so pupils can carry on being active outside school.
Use positive role models, such as older students, former pupils or coaches, to encourage others.
notes.tip: Exams ask for ways a school can increase participation. Give specific actions and say why each would work.

keyTerms.definition: A record of a person's physical activity history across their life so far, together with their current activity profile.
A description of the activities a person does now, how often, for how long and at what intensity.
A factor that helps a person take part in physical activity, such as facilities, teachers or family encouragement.
A factor that makes it harder for a person to take part in physical activity, such as cost, time or lack of facilities.
A device worn on the body that counts the steps taken and gives a measure of daily activity.
A written log in which a person records the type, duration and intensity of their activities over time.
Inaccuracy in information people give about themselves, caused by forgetting, guessing or giving answers they think are expected.
A small, guided group discussion used to explore the reasons and attitudes behind participation.
A Department of Education initiative recognising schools that promote physical activity and PE.
Whether the physical activity a programme started continues once the programme has ended.

questions.prompt: Discuss two different approaches to physical activity promotion.
questions.model: School-based programmes, such as the Active School Flag: the Department of Education recognises schools that promote physical activity and PE, so schools build activity into the timetable and the daily routine. Strength: it reaches every pupil, including those who would never join a club. Limitation: it ends when the pupil leaves school, so participation may not be sustained. Community events, such as parkrun: a free, weekly, timed 5 km event held on Saturday mornings that anyone can join. Strength: it is free and easy to join, so it reaches a wide range of people. Limitation: many of those who attend are already keen, so it may not reach inactive groups.

questions.prompt: Identify three methods of collecting data on physical activity participation and state what information each provides.
questions.model: 1. Pedometers: record the number of steps taken each day. They are cheap and objective, but they do not record cycling, swimming or intensity. 2. Activity diaries or logs: record the type, duration and intensity of each activity. They are detailed, but they depend on the honesty and memory of the person keeping them. 3. Questionnaires and surveys: record self-reported activity and attitudes from many people quickly, but results may be affected by self-report bias.

questions.prompt: Outline two supports and two barriers to physical activity participation in school.
questions.model: Support 1: PE classes taught by qualified teachers, which make activity enjoyable and accessible to every pupil. Support 2: school teams and after-school clubs, which give pupils organised activity beyond the timetable. Barrier 1: limited time for PE on the timetable, so pupils have few lessons to build skills and fitness. Barrier 2: exam pressure, especially in senior cycle, which pushes activity out of the school day.
